questions.question: An apple falls from a tree into the long grass. Over the next few weeks it goes soft and mushy, then slowly shrinks until almost nothing of it is left. What makes the apple rot?
questions.answer: Tiny living things feeding on it
choices: Tiny living things feeding on it
Rain and wind wearing it away
The Sun's heat drying it out
Time alone breaking it down
questions.context: Bacteria and moulds, most of them far too small to see, feed on the apple and break it down, and worms and insects help. Rain, wind and sunshine cannot make it rot on their own: an apple sealed away from all decomposers would not rot at all.
questions.grade_note: NSTA's Rotting Apple probe is written for grade 5 to check that students know living decomposers, not time or weather, make dead things rot.

questions.question: Every autumn the trees in a forest drop their leaves, and some of the forest's animals die. Suppose every decomposer in the forest vanished. What would happen there over the years that followed?
questions.answer: Dead plants and animals would pile up
choices: Dead plants and animals would pile up
The forest floor would stay clean and bare
The soil would grow richer every year
Dead plants would turn to soil faster
questions.context: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi, helped by earthworms and insects, break dead things down. Without them, leaves, logs and dead animals would pile higher every year, and the nutrients locked inside them would never get back to the soil for new plants.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-LS2-1 teaches 5th graders that fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms and return materials to the soil, and what a forest would be without them follows from it.

questions.question: A tree falls in a forest and slowly rots for many years, and young trees sprout along the soft, crumbling log. Besides water, what do the young trees take in from the rotting wood?
questions.answer: Nutrients set free from the wood
choices: Nutrients set free from the wood
Energy left over in the wood
Light stored up in the wood
Ready-made food from the wood
questions.context: Fungi, bacteria and insects break the log down and set free nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, which the young trees take in through their roots. The log gives them no energy and no food: plants make their own food in their leaves, using the energy of sunlight.
questions.grade_note: The National Park Service's Life in a Log lesson for grades 3 to 5 (NGSS 5-LS2-1) teaches the nurse log, and 5th graders learn that decomposers give plants matter, not energy.

questions.question: A gardener piles grass clippings, vegetable peels and dead leaves into a heap and keeps it damp. A few days later, the middle of the heap feels hot to the touch. What makes the heat?
questions.answer: Bacteria and fungi breaking it down
choices: Bacteria and fungi breaking it down
Sunlight soaked up by the dark heap
The heap's weight squeezing the middle
Warmth rising from the ground below
questions.context: Bacteria and fungi feed on the scraps, and as they break them down they give off heat, enough to warm the middle of a compost heap to 55 to 70 degrees Celsius. The heat comes from the decomposers at work, not from the Sun, the ground or the heap's weight.
questions.grade_note: FoodCorps's 5th-grade Break It Down lesson has students build a compost pile and graph its temperature as it heats up.

questions.question: A gardener is glad to find earthworms in her vegetable bed. They tunnel through the soil, swallowing dead leaves and bits of earth as they go. How do the earthworms help her plants?
questions.answer: Their droppings make the soil richer
choices: Their droppings make the soil richer
They eat the insects that harm roots
They keep moulds and bacteria away
They press the soil down firm and tight
questions.context: An earthworm's droppings, called castings, hold several times more nitrogen and phosphorus than the soil around them, and plants take those nutrients up through their roots. Earthworms eat dead plant matter and soil, not insects; their droppings are full of bacteria, and their tunnels loosen the soil and let air and water in.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade decomposer lessons such as the National Park Service's Life in a Log name earthworms among the living things that break dead matter down and return nutrients to the soil.

questions.question: Bacteria and fungi rot dead leaves much faster in some places than in others. Where would a fallen leaf usually rot away fastest?
questions.answer: On a warm, damp forest floor
choices: On a warm, damp forest floor
On a hot, dry desert floor
On a cold, dry mountainside
In a frozen field in winter
questions.context: Decomposers need water and warmth to grow and feed, so a leaf on a warm, wet rainforest floor can be gone within a year or two. Heat alone is not enough: in a dry desert the decomposers have too little water to work fast, and cold slows them down too.
questions.grade_note: 5th-grade compost and decomposition lessons teach that decomposers need water and warmth to do their work, and that a pile kept damp rots faster.

questions.question: A pumpkin is left in a garden after the harvest. It goes soft and rots, and a few months later almost nothing of it is left. Where did most of the pumpkin's matter go?
questions.answer: It went into the air and the soil
choices: It went into the air and the soil
It was used up and destroyed
It was changed into energy
It dried to dust and blew away
questions.context: Decomposers turn the pumpkin into carbon dioxide and water, which go into the air, and minerals, which stay in the soil. None of the matter is destroyed or turned into energy, and plants take it up and use it again; a rotting pumpkin sealed in a jar would weigh the same at the end as at the start.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-LS2-1 has 5th graders model matter moving from dead things into the air and soil, and grade-5 food-web lessons target the idea that rotting things simply disappear.

questions.question: As dead leaves, roots and small animals rot in the ground, decomposers turn what is left of them into a dark, crumbly part of the soil, rich in nutrients. What is this part of the soil called?
choices: Humus
Clay
Silt
Sand
questions.context: Humus is the dark brown or black part of the soil made from decayed plants and animals, and it holds nutrients and water for plant roots. Clay, silt and sand are different: they are tiny bits of rock, broken down over thousands of years.
questions.grade_note: National Geographic's humus entry is written for grades 5 to 8, and soil built from decayed remains is part of 5th-grade decomposer units (NGSS 5-LS2-1).
